item.title: Spark ML
item.description:
Spark includes a machine-learning library named MLlib. The phrase “Spark ML” is commonly used for MLlib’s DataFrame-based API because its Java and Scala classes live under org.apache.spark.ml and its Python classes under pyspark.ml.

These names are easy to confuse:

Name Meaning
MLlib Spark’s complete machine-learning library
spark.ml The primary, DataFrame-based MLlib API
spark.mllib The older RDD-based API, now in maintenance mode
Spark ML An informal name for the spark.ml API

spark.mllib is not removed, but new application code should normally use spark.ml. The DataFrame API integrates with Spark SQL, has a consistent pipeline model, and provides similar APIs across Java, Scala, and Python.

item.title: Apache Flink and Kafka Integration
item.description:
Apache Flink is a distributed processing engine for stateful computations over bounded and unbounded data streams. It can consume events as they arrive, maintain application state, use event time, recover from failures, and continuously publish results.

Apache Kafka is a distributed event-streaming platform. Producers append records to partitioned topics, Kafka retains those records, and consumers read them at their own pace. Kafka is commonly the durable transport layer in a streaming architecture, while Flink performs the computation:

item.title: LangGraph4j
item.description:
LangGraph4j is a Java library for building stateful, graph-based AI applications. A graph consists of nodes that perform work, edges that select the next node, and shared state that changes as the graph runs. It is inspired by LangGraph and integrates with LangChain4j and Spring AI, but a graph node can also be ordinary Java code.

text 
 +------------+
 | call model |
 +------+-----+
 |
 tool requested?
 / \
 yes no
 / \
 +-------v-------+ +--v--+
 | execute tool | | END |
 +-------+-------+ +-----+
 |
 +----------> call model

Cycles are intentional. They let an application reason, act, inspect a result, and reason again. LangGraph4j makes that control flow and its state explicit; it also provides reducers, conditional routing, checkpoints, breakpoints, streaming, graph visualization, and subgraphs.

item.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
item.description:
Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, retrieves information from an external corpus and supplies selected evidence to a generative model for one request.

A minimal RAG system has two paths:

text 
Indexing path

documents -> parse -> normalize -> split -> embed -> index

Request path

question -> retrieve -> rank -> select context -> generate -> answer

RAG does not modify the language model’s parameters. It changes the input context presented to the model. This makes it useful for information that is:

item.title: AgentScope
item.description:
AgentScope is an open-source framework for building and operating applications in which a large language model can reason, call tools, retain state, and collaborate with users or other agents. It was initiated by Alibaba and is available as separate Python and Java projects.

An ordinary model call has a short, application-controlled path:

text 
application -> prompt -> model -> response

An agent adds an execution loop:

text 
user goal
 |
 v
model reasons -> chooses a tool -> application executes it
 ^ |
 +----------- tool result <---------+
 |
 v
final answer, interruption, or next action

The model still does not execute Java or Python functions by itself. It emits a structured request, and AgentScope validates and dispatches that request through its tool system. The framework also manages the messages, event stream, permissions, session state, and repeated model calls around that loop.

item.title: Vector Stores
item.description:
A vector store stores numeric vectors and retrieves the items whose vectors are nearest to a query vector. In AI applications, those vectors are commonly embeddings: compact numeric representations of text, images, audio, users, products, or other objects.

Vector stores make questions such as these practical:

  • Which documentation passages are semantically related to this question?
  • Which products resemble the one a customer is viewing?
  • Have we processed a support ticket with the same meaning before?
  • Which tools are relevant to the user’s current goal?
  • Which saved memories may matter in this conversation?

A vector store is not a language model, and it does not generate an answer. It is a retrieval component. It finds candidate data; application code or a model then decides how to use that data.

item.title: JUnit 5 Architecture, Maven Setup, and JUnit 4 Migration
item.description:
JUnit 5 separates the API used to write tests from the infrastructure that discovers and executes them. The separation lets Maven, IDEs, and custom launchers run several test models through one interface.

The examples target JUnit 5.13.4. JUnit 6 retains the same architecture, but a project that must remain on JUnit 5 should use the versioned JUnit 5 documentation.

Platform, Jupiter, and Vintage #

JUnit 5 consists of three components:

item.title: Mockito without and with JUnit 5
item.description:
Mockito creates test doubles for Java interfaces and classes. Its core API does not depend on JUnit: a program can create a mock, configure behavior, invoke code, and verify interactions from an ordinary main method. JUnit integration adds test discovery and automatic mock lifecycle management rather than basic mocking capability.

Minimal Maven Project Without JUnit #

Put the demonstration under src/test/java because Mockito has test scope:

text 
mockito-hello/
├── pom.xml
└── src/test/java/com/example/MockitoHello.java
xml 
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
 xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
 xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
 <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

 <groupId>com.example</groupId>
 <artifactId>mockito-hello</artifactId>
 <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

 <properties>
 <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release>
 <mockito.version>5.23.0</mockito.version>
 </properties>

 <dependencies>
 <dependency>
 <groupId>org.mockito</groupId>
 <artifactId>mockito-core</artifactId>
 <version>${mockito.version}</version>
 <scope>test</scope>
 </dependency>
 </dependencies>
</project>
java 
package com.example;

import static org.mockito.Mockito.mock;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.verify;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.when;

interface Greeter {
 String greet(String name);
}

public final class MockitoHello {
 public static void main(String[] args) {
 Greeter greeter = mock(Greeter.class);
 when(greeter.greet("Ada")).thenReturn("Hello, Ada");

 String actual = greeter.greet("Ada");
 if (!"Hello, Ada".equals(actual)) {
 throw new AssertionError("unexpected result: " + actual);
 }

 verify(greeter).greet("Ada");
 }
}

item.title: Testing Spring Boot REST APIs
item.description:
Testing a Spring Boot REST API requires several scopes because a direct Java call, a simulated MVC request, and a request through a live server exercise different failure boundaries. A useful test suite places most behavior checks below the Spring context, then adds narrower web slices and a smaller number of full-application tests.

The dependency examples target Spring Boot 3.x because its test starter uses JUnit 5. Spring Boot 4 manages JUnit 6; Jupiter concepts remain, but package names for several Boot test annotations changed.

item.title: Java Date and Time
item.description:
Datetime-related SDKs.

Time zone is an artificial concept, and only matters when a specific locale is concerned.

Contrary to intuition, the phrase local time means timezone-irrelevant, i.e. the class in question has no field storing timezone information.

Before Java 8: java.util.Date & Java.util.Calendar #

Java 8 and Later: java.time.* #

interface Temporal & final Class Instant Implements Temporal #

A Temporal instance represents an instant in an arbitrary time range. An amount of time can be added to this, subtracted from this, yet still produce a Temporal

item.title: Using Thymeleaf without Spring MVC
item.description:
Thymeleaf can render HTML in a batch job, command-line program, mail service, or report pipeline without Spring MVC. A standalone application configures a template resolver and TemplateEngine, supplies a context, and writes the rendered output to its destination.

Choose the Integration Level #

A non-Spring program needs the core Thymeleaf artifact:

xml 
<dependency>
 <groupId>org.thymeleaf</groupId>
 <artifactId>thymeleaf</artifactId>
 <version>3.1.3.RELEASE</version>
</dependency>

A Spring application can use thymeleaf-spring6 and SpringTemplateEngine for Spring EL, MessageSource, conversion, and Spring-aware link behavior. Spring Boot dependency management should choose the matching Thymeleaf version. spring-boot-starter-thymeleaf is convenient when those integrations are needed, but it is not required to run the core engine and does not require MVC.

item.title: Spring Environment and Profiles
item.description:
Spring’s Environment combines two concerns: resolving configuration properties and determining which bean-definition profiles are active. The core framework defines the abstraction and standard JVM/servlet sources; Spring Boot adds its own external-configuration sources and precedence rules.

Property Sources and Precedence #

A configurable environment owns ordered PropertySource<?> objects in MutablePropertySources. Resolution searches from highest to lowest precedence and returns the first source containing the requested key. Naming and ordering sources explicitly avoids configuration that changes with registration order:

item.title: Jakarta Persistence, Hibernate, and Spring Data JPA
item.description:
Jakarta Persistence defines the standard Java API for object-relational mapping. Hibernate is a widely used implementation. Spring Data JPA builds repository abstractions on top of a Jakarta Persistence provider.

The Jakarta Persistence Model #

An application maps ordinary classes to database tables with annotations such as @Entity, @Table, @Id, and @Column:

java 
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class PurchaseOrder {
 @Id
 @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
 private Long id;

 @Column(nullable = false)
 private String status;
}

The standard APIs live in jakarta.persistence. An implementation discovers a jakarta.persistence.spi.PersistenceProvider through Java’s service-provider mechanism. The provider translates persistence operations and JPQL or Criteria queries into database-specific SQL.

item.title: Java Modules
item.description:
The Java Platform Module System (JPMS) makes dependencies and package encapsulation explicit. A named module contains a descriptor, module-info.java, at its source root. Compiling it produces module-info.class in an exploded module directory or modular JAR.

java 
module com.example.app {
 requires com.example.codec;
 uses com.example.codec.Decoder;
}

module com.example.codec {
 exports com.example.codec.api;
 exports com.example.codec.internal to com.example.app;
 opens com.example.codec.model to com.example.json;
 provides com.example.codec.Decoder with com.example.codec.JsonDecoder;
}

Compilation, Packaging, and Launch #

A conventional multi-module source tree has one directory per module below the module source path. Compile with:

item.title: Colorful Terminal Output with Jansi
item.description:
Jansi is a Java library for generating and processing ANSI escape sequences. These sequences let a terminal display colors and styles, move the cursor, erase parts of the screen, and perform other terminal operations.

For example, the following bytes mean “use bold red text,” print FAILED, and then restore the terminal’s default attributes:

text 
\u001B[1;31mFAILED\u001B[0m

Writing those codes by hand is difficult to read and easy to get wrong. Jansi provides a fluent Java API for constructing them and terminal-aware streams that can pass through, adapt, or remove them as appropriate.

item.title: Spring Bean Lifecycle and Prototype Scope
item.description:
Spring separates bean metadata from bean instances. A BeanDefinition describes how to create an object, while a BeanFactory applies that definition when the object is requested. An ApplicationContext adds coordinated startup, post-processing, events, resource loading, and shutdown.

What Happens During Context Refresh #

AbstractApplicationContext.refresh() prepares the environment and bean factory before application singletons become usable. The major stages are:

  1. Prepare or obtain the BeanFactory and load bean definitions.
  2. Invoke BeanFactoryPostProcessors, including configuration-class processing, while definitions can still be changed.
  3. Discover and register BeanPostProcessors.
  4. Initialize context infrastructure such as message resolution, events, and context-specific resources.
  5. Instantiate the remaining non-lazy singleton beans.
  6. Publish the refreshed state and ContextRefreshedEvent.

A BeanFactoryPostProcessor changes metadata. A BeanPostProcessor instead sees instances and can inject fields, invoke lifecycle annotations, or replace a bean with a proxy. Creating ordinary application beans from a factory post-processor is unsafe because it can instantiate them before all post-processors are registered.

item.title: MyBatis Mapping
item.description:
MyBatis maps Java calls to SQL statements while JDBC owns parameter binding, statement execution, and result-set access. A mapper should make that boundary visible: SQL column names belong in the statement, Java property names belong in parameter and result mappings, and a type handler performs any nonstandard conversion between them.

Parameter and Result Boundaries #

Simple parameters can use #{id} placeholders. Object and map parameters expose named properties, while multiple mapper parameters should use @Param so the names do not depend on compiler metadata:

item.title: Maven
item.description:
Maven builds a project by executing plugin goals in lifecycle order. A lifecycle contains ordered phases; invoking a phase executes that phase and every earlier phase in the same lifecycle. Plugins contribute goals, and lifecycle bindings select the goals that run for a project packaging.

Project Model and Coordinates #

The POM identifies an artifact by groupId, artifactId, version, and packaging. Parent POMs, dependency management, and imported BOMs centralize versions without adding an artifact to the classpath. dependencyManagement therefore constrains dependencies only after a child declares them.

item.title: Spring Annotation Processing
item.description:
Spring uses annotations as declarative metadata for component discovery, configuration, dependency injection, transactions, web request mapping, and other framework services. Java reflection exposes the raw annotations; Spring adds a consistent model for composed annotations, aliases, search strategies, and metadata reading without loading classes.

Java Annotation Semantics #

An annotation declaration is itself an interface whose implicit superinterface is java.lang.annotation.Annotation:

java 
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
public @interface Audited {
}

Runtime reflection can inspect @Audited when it is directly present on a class. Meta-annotations such as @Retention, @Target, and @Documented describe an annotation declaration but do not cause arbitrary transitive lookup.

item.title: Java Logging with SLF4J and Log4j 2
item.description:
SLF4J is a logging API facade. Application code should depend on slf4j-api, while deployment selects one compatible provider such as Log4j 2 or Logback. SLF4J 2 discovers providers through ServiceLoader; retain exactly one. With Log4j 2, log4j-slf4j2-impl adapts SLF4J to Log4j Core. Do not combine it with log4j-to-slf4j, because events then re-enter the facade and form a bridge loop.

java 
private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(Orders.class);
log.info("Accepted order {}", orderId);
log.warn("Order {} failed validation", orderId, exception);

Parameterized messages defer formatting while the level is disabled. Use an explicit exception argument rather than interpolating a stack trace into text.

item.title: Servlets and Tomcat
item.description:
The Jakarta Servlet API defines a server-side request and response model. Apache Tomcat implements that API and supplies the Catalina servlet container, HTTP and AJP connectors, session management, deployment, and operational tooling. Tomcat 11 implements Jakarta Servlet 6.1 and requires Java 17; older applications that import javax.servlet.* need migration to the jakarta.servlet.* namespace or an older compatible container.

Web Application Layout #

A deployable web application can be an expanded directory or a WAR archive:

item.title: Spring Overview and Transactions
item.description:
Spring Framework provides a dependency-injection container plus focused modules for AOP, data access, transactions, messaging, and web applications. Transaction management demonstrates the framework’s integration model: application code declares a boundary, while an interceptor coordinates a resource-specific PlatformTransactionManager or reactive transaction manager.

Proxy-Based Declarative Transactions #

With the default advice mode, Spring wraps an eligible bean in an AOP proxy. Calls entering a method matched by @Transactional pass through TransactionInterceptor, which reads transaction metadata, starts or joins a transaction, invokes the target, and commits or rolls back.

item.title: Grizzly HTTP Server
item.description:
Grizzly is a Java NIO networking framework maintained by the Eclipse EE4J project. Its grizzly-framework module builds on Java’s non-blocking I/O APIs; it is not a direct wrapper around a particular operating-system API such as epoll.

Modules #

Common Grizzly modules include:

  • grizzly-http, which provides HTTP protocol support;
  • grizzly-http-server, an embeddable HTTP server with Grizzly’s own API; and
  • grizzly-http-servlet, which provides servlet-related integration.

Grizzly is used by GlassFish and can also run small embedded services. It is an HTTP server, not a Jakarta REST implementation. Combine it with Jersey when serving JAX-RS resources.

item.title: Java Launcher Options
item.description:
The java launcher starts a JVM implementation; many flags are HotSpot implementation options rather than Java language or JVM specification requirements. Use the launcher documentation for the JDK release deployed by the application, because availability and defaults change between releases.

Option Families #

Standard options include --class-path, --module-path, -Dname=value, and -version. HotSpot uses -X for nonstandard options and -XX: for diagnostic and advanced flags. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prepends options to every launcher invocation in its environment, so reserve it for controlled runtime environments and inspect it when a process has unexpected behavior.

item.title: Java Generics
item.description:
Java generics provide compile-time type checking while preserving compatibility with pre-generics bytecode. The compiler erases type arguments, inserts casts where required, and may generate bridge methods to preserve overriding after erasure. Consequently List<String> and List<Integer> have the same runtime class, and generic type arguments cannot reliably be recovered from an object.

Invariance and Bounds #

Generic classes are invariant: List<Integer> is not a List<Number>, because the latter would permit inserting a Double. Wildcards express variance at an API boundary.

item.title: JVM Garbage Collection
item.description:
The JVM Specification requires automatic storage management but does not prescribe a collector or heap layout. Collector behavior is therefore a property of the deployed JVM, release, flags, heap size, and workload.

Reachability and Memory Pools #

Tracing begins from GC roots, including live thread stacks and registers, static fields, JNI handles, and VM runtime structures. An object strongly reachable from a root remains live. Soft references may be cleared under memory pressure, weak references do not retain their referents, and phantom references support post-mortem coordination through ReferenceQueue. None is a substitute for deterministic resource cleanup; use try-with-resources and Cleaner only as a safety net. Finalization is deprecated for removal.

item.title: Project Reactor
item.description:
Project Reactor is a Java library for composing asynchronous and event-driven programs. Its core types, Mono<T> and Flux<T>, describe computations that may produce values later rather than returning those values immediately.

Reactor is the reactive foundation used by Spring WebFlux. It is also useful outside HTTP servers for asynchronous clients, event streams, messaging, concurrent orchestration, and any pipeline whose inputs may arrive over time.

The important word is describe. This code does not fetch a user when the line is evaluated:

item.title: JVM Architecture
item.description:
The JVM Specification defines an abstract execution model, not an operating system memory map. An implementation may use JIT compilation, moving garbage collection, contiguous or segmented storage, and native metadata while preserving the specified behavior.

Runtime Data Areas #

Each JVM thread has a program-counter register, a JVM stack, and optionally a native-method stack. The PC identifies the current JVM instruction for Java code and has an undefined value while native code executes. A JVM stack holds frames; failure to create a frame produces StackOverflowError for a size limit or OutOfMemoryError when an expandable stack cannot grow.

item.title: JVM Classfile Format
item.description:
A class file is a big-endian binary structure consumed by the JVM. It begins with 0xCAFEBABE, followed by u2 minor and major versions. A JVM accepts only the versions defined for its implementation; class-file parsers must reject unsupported versions rather than assume that a newer file is backward-compatible.

Top-Level Structure #

After the magic and version, the file contains:

  1. constant_pool_count and the indexed constant-pool entries;
  2. class access_flags, this_class, and super_class;
  3. interface indexes;
  4. field_info structures;
  5. method_info structures; and
  6. class-level attribute_info structures.

Counts are unsigned u2 values, except an attribute’s attribute_length, which is u4. Access flags describe the context: ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_FINAL, ACC_SUPER, ACC_INTERFACE, ACC_ABSTRACT, ACC_SYNTHETIC, ACC_ANNOTATION, ACC_ENUM, and ACC_MODULE are not all meaningful or legal for every class-file kind.

item.title: Java Service Provider Interface
item.description:
Java SPI separates a service contract from one or more providers and from the consumer that selects them. The consumer depends on the service type and uses ServiceLoader, so providers can be added at deployment without an application dependency on concrete classes.

Classpath Services #

Before modules, a provider JAR listed implementations in META-INF/services/<fully.qualified.ServiceName>. The UTF-8 file has one provider class name per line; blank lines and # comments are allowed. Each provider must be accessible to the loader used for discovery and offer a public no-argument constructor.

item.title: JAX-RS and Jersey
item.description:
JAX-RS is the Jakarta standard API and specification for HTTP resources in the jakarta.ws.rs packages. It defines annotations, request and response types, client APIs, providers, and server-sent event support. Jersey is a conforming JAX-RS implementation.

JAX-RS is distinct from JAX-WS, which concerns XML web services.

Define Resources #

Add the Jakarta REST API at compile time and a JAX-RS implementation at runtime. A resource class uses @Path; methods use an HTTP method annotation and may add a relative path:

item.title: Java Enums and Interfaces
item.description:
An enum declaration defines a final class with a fixed set of instances. Each constant is an instance of that class, which conceptually extends Enum<E> with the enum type as E; no user enum may extend another class. The compiler supplies values() and valueOf(String), while Enum supplies the name, ordinal, comparison, and serialization rules.

Interfaces and Constant-Specific Behavior #

An enum may implement interfaces, and the implementation can be shared by all constants or supplied in a constant-specific class body.

item.title: Spring Resources
item.description:
org.springframework.core.io.Resource gives Spring APIs one handle for content that may reside in a file, classpath entry, URL, servlet context, byte array, or already-open stream. The abstraction describes access capabilities; it does not make every resource seekable, repeatable, writable, or backed by a file.

The Resource Contract #

Resource extends InputStreamSource. getInputStream() is the fundamental operation, while methods such as exists(), isReadable(), isOpen(), isFile(), contentLength(), lastModified(), and getDescription() expose capabilities or metadata.

item.title: Spring Container Types
item.description:
Spring’s container API has three distinct layers: bean metadata, the factory that creates objects from that metadata, and an application context that coordinates the factory with application services. Keeping those layers separate makes Spring source code and extension points easier to reason about.

Bean Definitions and Registries #

BeanDefinition is mutable metadata for one bean. It records the bean class or class name, scope, constructor arguments, property values, qualifiers, factory method, lifecycle methods, role, source location, and explicit dependencies. The parent/child metadata relationship is independent of Java inheritance.

item.title: Spring Conversion and Validation
item.description:
Spring treats conversion, presentation formatting, object binding, and validation as separate operations. A request parameter can therefore become a typed property and still produce structured errors without coupling the domain object to a web controller.

Conversion and Formatting #

ConversionService is the facade for type conversion. It can first answer whether a conversion is available and then convert by raw class or by TypeDescriptor, which preserves annotations and nested generic information.

item.title: Spring MVC
item.description:
Spring MVC is the Servlet-based web framework in Spring Framework. Its front controller, DispatcherServlet, coordinates request mapping, argument resolution, controller invocation, return-value handling, and exception translation. Spring WebFlux uses a different reactive runtime and threading model; the two frameworks must not be treated as interchangeable.

Bootstrap and Dispatch #

A non-Boot Servlet application can register a web application context and dispatcher through WebApplicationInitializer:

java 
public final class WebInitializer implements WebApplicationInitializer {
 @Override
 public void onStartup(ServletContext servletContext) {
 var context = new AnnotationConfigWebApplicationContext();
 context.register(WebConfiguration.class);

 var servlet = servletContext.addServlet(
 "mvc", new DispatcherServlet(context));
 servlet.setLoadOnStartup(1);
 servlet.addMapping("/");
 }
}

Spring Boot performs equivalent registration for an MVC application. Mapping the dispatcher to / lets the Servlet container retain special handling for static resources and JSPs; /* also captures those dispatches.

item.title: Kotlin for Java Programmers
item.description:
Kotlin compiles to JVM bytecode and interoperates directly with Java, while adding null safety, concise declarations, extension functions, and structured concurrency.

Classes and Constructors #

A class has one primary constructor in its header and may have secondary constructors in its body. Primary-constructor parameters become properties only when marked val or var; initialization code belongs in an init block.

kotlin 
class Account(val id: String, initialBalance: Int) {
 var balance = initialBalance
 private set

 init {
 require(initialBalance >= 0)
 }

 constructor(id: String) : this(id, 0)
}

Secondary constructors must delegate to the primary constructor, directly or through another secondary constructor. Prefer the primary constructor plus default parameters when that expresses the API clearly.

item.title: Java Class Loading
item.description:
Class loading converts a binary representation into a Class object. Linking and initialization are separate steps, thus loading a type does not imply that its static initializer has run.

Loaders and Type Identity #

The JDK supplies bootstrap, platform, and application loaders. The bootstrap loader defines core platform classes and is represented by null in selected APIs; the platform loader defines platform modules; the application loader loads application classes from the class path or module path. Custom loaders commonly use parent-first delegation:

item.title: Spring Thread Pools
item.description:
Spring’s TaskExecutor abstracts task submission. The common ThreadPoolTaskExecutor is a managed JavaBean wrapper around ThreadPoolExecutor; its pool, queue, rejection, and lifecycle choices still determine system capacity.

Defining and Naming an Executor #

Name executors by workload so callers select the intended resource:

java 
@Bean("reportExecutor")
ThreadPoolTaskExecutor reportExecutor() {
 var executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
 executor.setCorePoolSize(8);
 executor.setMaxPoolSize(24);
 executor.setQueueCapacity(100);
 executor.setKeepAliveSeconds(30);
 executor.setThreadNamePrefix("report-");
 executor.setRejectedExecutionHandler(
 new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
 return executor;
}

Spring initializes and shuts down a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor as a managed bean. Returning its concrete type preserves lifecycle configuration and monitoring methods. Separate executors isolate workloads with different latency, blocking, priority, or downstream-capacity requirements.

item.title: Spring Data JPA Specification API
item.description:
When a Spring Data JPA repository needs a WHERE clause that is optional, composable, and decided at runtime, the usual API is org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaSpecificationExecutor<T>.

It is the bridge between:

  1. Spring Data repository methods such as findAll(...), count(...), and exists(...)
  2. Spring’s org.springframework.data.jpa.domain.Specification<T>
  3. the Jakarta Persistence Criteria API centered around jakarta.persistence.criteria.CriteriaBuilder

JpaSpecificationExecutor<T> #

Suppose we have an entity:

java 
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class PurchaseOrder {
 @Id
 private Long id;

 @Column(nullable = false)
 private String status;

 @Column(nullable = false)
 private String customerEmail;

 @Column(nullable = false)
 private Instant createdAt;

 @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
 private Customer customer;
}

and a repository:

item.title: Java Design Patterns
item.description:
Patterns name recurring design trade-offs. Java language features can implement a pattern, but neither a lambda nor a dependency-injection container is itself a replacement for a design decision.

Creational Patterns #

A Factory centralizes construction when callers must not depend on a concrete type or construction selects an implementation. A factory hides useful details, but a factory with a method for every product can become an unnecessary indirection.

java 
interface Parser { Document parse(String text); }
final class Parsers {
 static Parser forFormat(Format format) { return format::parse; }
}

A Builder collects optional arguments and validates cross-field invariants before producing an immutable value. Use a constructor or static factory when there are few mandatory fields; a builder that only mirrors setters obscures the required state. A Prototype is often clearer in Java as an explicit copy constructor or copyOf factory than Cloneable, whose shallow-copy and inheritance semantics are difficult to extend safely.

item.title: Gradle
item.description:
Gradle is a build automation tool for JVM projects and many other ecosystems. Build logic is written in the Groovy DSL (.gradle) or Kotlin DSL (.gradle.kts). Gradle itself runs on the JVM.

Project Files #

From a repository root, the important files are:

  • settings.gradle[.kts] defines the build and includes subprojects. It is required for a multi-project build and may set the root project name.
  • build.gradle[.kts] defines plugins, dependencies, tasks, and conventions for the root project or a subproject.
  • gradle.properties holds project properties. User-wide properties may live in ~/.gradle/gradle.properties.
  • gradlew, gradlew.bat, and gradle/wrapper/ form the Gradle Wrapper and should be committed.
  • .gradle/ is local Gradle state and should be ignored.

Use include("service", "web") in settings.gradle.kts to register subprojects. Each subproject can have its own build script while sharing repository-wide conventions.

item.title: Java Concurrency and Executors
item.description:
Executor separates submitting a Runnable from deciding where it runs. ExecutorService adds lifecycle management and submit; Callable<V> can return a value or throw a checked exception, and Future<V> represents the eventual result. Future.get() establishes the required visibility of actions performed by the task before completion.

java 
Future<Result> future = pool.submit(() -> compute(input));

Use synchronized, Lock, atomics, concurrent collections, or message passing to establish happens-before relationships. An executor supplies scheduling, not automatic safety for mutable shared objects.

item.title: Java Standard Library
item.description:
Small library contracts frequently determine correctness more than API surface area. The following rules prevent common Java integration failures.

Object Contracts #

equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and false for null. If two objects are equal, they must have the same hashCode; therefore override both before using a value as a hash key. Do not mutate equality fields while an object is a map key. Prefer composition over inheritance when equality would otherwise break symmetry.

item.title: Java History and Platform
item.description: Sun Microsystems released Java 1.0 in 1996. Major compatibility milestones include J2SE 1.2 (1998), Java 5 (2004, generics and annotations), Java 8 (2014, lambdas), and Java 9 (2017, modules). Oracle acquired Sun in 2010. OpenJDK is the open-source reference implementation of Java SE, with HotSpot as its principal JVM implementation; Oracle JDK and many vendor distributions are builds of OpenJDK with differing support and packaging policies. Since Java 10, feature releases follow a six-month cadence, while chosen releases receive longer vendor support.

item.title: Micrometer Application Observability
item.description:
Micrometer is a collection of Java libraries for instrumenting applications. It provides vendor-neutral APIs for metrics, observations, and distributed tracing, along with adapters that connect those APIs to monitoring systems such as Prometheus and tracing implementations such as OpenTelemetry.

Micrometer is not a monitoring server. It does not store telemetry, execute PromQL, render dashboards, or deliver alerts. It runs inside an application and produces telemetry for other systems to collect:

item.title: Java Annotations
item.description:
An annotation is metadata attached to a declaration or type use. It is not a general-purpose object literal: an annotation type is a special interface whose members describe the permitted metadata.

Declaring Annotation Types #

Annotation members have no parameters or type parameters, and may not declare a throws clause. A member type is limited to a primitive, String, Class, an enum type, an annotation type, or a one-dimensional array of one of those types. Values must be compile-time constants, class literals, enum constants, annotations, or arrays thereof. null is never an annotation element value.
